c6e7cabff185da96: An extract from Plato's "Republic" reads: "Said the old Cephalus to the younger Socrates, 'Older men of my age flock together and in our meeting my common tale is – I cannot eat, I cannot drink, the pleasure of youth and love have fled away, there was a good time once, but now gone, and life is no longer ours.'"
Such is the reality of ageing, and perhaps there is a lesson here for politicians who have overstayed their welcome in the political arena.
I hope that the impending Melaka state election will be an eye-opener for Malaysians, particularly our political leaders who seem to have difficulty recognising when it is time to call it a day.
PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang and many politicians of his generation should seriously consider retiring from politics.
Judging from their regular outbursts and political pronouncements, some appear increasingly disconnected from the realities, aspirations and concerns of ordinary Malaysians.
Their political vocabulary, arguments and preoccupations seem to belong to another era.
Hadi's latest outburst is a case in point.
In his reaction to the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) between opposition MPs and the government, he likened the arrangement to the deception of the Dajjal.

Whatever one's views about the CSA, surely there are more constructive ways to debate a parliamentary arrangement. It is one thing to disagree with a political agreement; it is quite another to invoke apocalyptic religious imagery to discredit it.
Such rhetoric does little to advance public understanding or the quality of our political discourse.
Malaysia is rapidly changing
This is precisely the problem with some of our ageing political leaders. They seem more interested in fighting yesterday's political battles than addressing tomorrow's challenges.
Our younger population is concerned about employment, housing affordability, wages, education, technology, artificial intelligence, green agenda and the rising cost of living.
They want practical solutions, economic opportunities and a government that understands the world they are growing up in.
Yet much of our political conversation remains trapped in old rivalries, identity politics, religious arguments and endless disputes over who should be in power and who should become prime minister.
How much longer must Malaysians listen to identity and religious politics from the same personalities with the same political arguments?

Hadi is not alone. Former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, deputy prime minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, former federal minister Rais Yatim and several other long-serving political figures should seriously consider leaving the political arena as well.

They have had their opportunities, occupied important positions and exercised considerable influence over the country's political upheavals. They should recognise that political leadership is not a lifetime entitlement.

There is a difference between serving the country and holding on to political power. After decades in politics, surely there comes a time when personal ambition must give way to institutional renewal.

Our political parties should not be personal properties, nor should their leadership positions become permanent appointments. No individual should be indispensable to a political party, let alone to an entire nation.
Malaysia's political weakness

One of Malaysia's biggest political weaknesses is the reluctance of senior politicians to groom and give way to younger leaders. They continue to dominate party structures, determine candidate selections and control political narratives.
Young politicians are often expected to wait patiently for their turn, while the same senior personalities continue to occupy the top positions election after election.
This is unhealthy.
A political party cannot produce new leaders or renew its leadership in a hierarchy that is dominated by ageing politicians. PAS, Bersatu and Umno are clear examples.
Do they genuinely believe in the future of their parties or are they simply protecting their own positions?
I fully agree with the argument about giving younger politicians greater opportunities.

The emergence of younger leaders should not merely be an electoral gimmick to attract younger voters. They must be given real responsibilities, decision-making authority and opportunities to shape national policies.
Of course, being young does not automatically make someone a capable leader. Experience, integrity, competence and sound judgment matter.

But these qualities cannot be the exclusive possessions of older politicians, either. Young leaders need opportunities to acquire experience, and they cannot do so if the older generation refuses to release its grip.

Let the younger generation make mistakes, learn from them and develop their own leadership capabilities. That is how political maturity is built. We cannot keep telling young people that they lack experience while denying them the opportunity to gain it.

There is also a larger democratic question. How can we expect a country to embrace new ideas, modernise its institutions and prepare for the future when much of its political leadership remains occupied by personalities whose political careers began several decades ago?
The world is moving on
Technology, economic structures, international competition and the expectations of younger citizens are changing. Political leadership must change with them.
For Hadi, Muhyiddin, Zahid and scores of others who have spent much of their lives in politics, perhaps the greatest contribution they can now make is to step aside gracefully.

They can offer advice, share their experience and allow the next generation to take responsibility. They do not need to remain party presidents, political kingmakers or permanent fixtures in our national politics.

The Melaka election should be more than another contest between political coalitions. It should also be an opportunity for voters to consider the kind of leadership they want for the next decade and beyond.

Malaysia needs a political generation that looks forward, not backwards; one that debates policies rather than personalities, solves problems rather than manufactures controversies, and builds institutions rather than protects individual political careers.
Enough is enough. You have had your time. You have had your opportunities. It is time to let go.

3b237e183dd5187e: Malaysians have come to take our festivals for granted, gliding through Deepavali as if it were just another ordinary day on the calendar—a polite pause amid the roar of traffic and the clatter of daily life.

Yet, if we close our eyes for a moment and picture it—houses alive with oil lamps glowing in every direction, the air fragrant with sesame-scented murukku, and the laughter of children in new clothes spilling onto the streets—we are reminded of the festival's vibrant soul.
What few of us realise, however, is that this radiant celebration once rose in daring rebellion.
Today, Deepavali burns brightly as a public holiday across Peninsular Malaysia, with Sabah having quietly folded it into its own calendar of observances.

But few know the breathless, dramatic saga of how this festival was once locked in a fierce, cinematic battle for supremacy—not merely over lamps and sweets, but for the very right to be recognised as a national holiday.
That epic contest was fought not against external forces, but between two towering pillars of the Hindu community itself: Deepavali and Thaipusam.

Both claimed the same prize: a full public holiday so their celebrations could soar to their unbridled heights. One side believed Deepavali, with its blaze of lights that welcomed every soul under the sun, was the broader, more inclusive flame that would carry Indian identity into the future. The other saw in Thaipusam—with its profound message of inner victory through devotion and discipline—the sacred, undying fire that needed to be nurtured.
The battle was real, heated, and decided in colonial Singapore in 1914—a moment that still echoes today, though almost all of us remain blissfully unaware of it.
I wonder how many Malaysians—Indians among them—know that the first Indian-related public holiday in British Malaya was actually for Thaipusam?

Then spelled Tai-pusum, it first flickered into existence in the 1879 Holidays Ordinance IX as a bank holiday in Penang. In British Malaya, bank holidays existed primarily to ensure the colony's commercial engine paused simultaneously.

Thaipusam secured its spot because of a dynamic Indian merchant class in Penang and because government departments, most notably the Public Works Department and the municipal council, were overwhelmingly staffed by Indians.

Then came 1914. The colonial administration decided that one set of uniform public holidays should cover the entire Straits Settlements. Operating under the rule of "one major festival of each of the main races," a Bill was drafted nominating Thaipusam for the Indian community as it was already a holiday in Penang.

Here the story takes a twist. The English-speaking elites and merchants of Singapore preferred Deepavali. Their community was a diverse tapestry woven from Telugus, Gujaratis, Sindhis, Malayalees, and Punjabis—not just Tamils. Thaipusam, they argued, was too narrow, too tied to the Chettiar community, and too purely religious for their cosmopolitan vision.
Led by the formidable Dr N Veerasamy Naidu—one of Singapore’s first Indian doctors and a municipal commissioner—the merchant group petitioned Governor Sir Arthur Henderson Young.

Their letter glowed with eloquence and loyalty, speaking of making Deepavali “an act of grace which will be greatly appreciated not only by the 60 or 70,000 most loyal and submissive subjects of His most gracious Majesty the Emperor of India but by the future generations of the permanent residents of the colony”.
They reminded the governor that Deepavali was already observed as a public holiday in India and that it was a public holiday in Singapore in the year 1912.

The movement quickly gained momentum. In February 1914, roughly a thousand prominent Hindus packed the Hindu Association on Belilios Road. Veerasamy, who chaired the meeting, reminded those present that Deepavali had been declared a holiday in Singapore in 1912, thanks to an earlier petition through the Hindu and Muhammadan Endowments Board. Yet a similar application in 1913 had not succeeded.
Now the stakes were higher — the holiday would cover the whole colony. And it would not require annual petitions.

Among those present were influential merchants and elites such as MV Pillay, SMR Naidu, KN Kothary, Nagar Das, Chotiirmal, M Soomapah, Mungul Singh, Dr Bardhan, Veer Singh, Thambyrajah, Veeraragava Aiyar, Singaram Pillai and Sivakadacha Padayachi.

Leaders like MV Pillay argued passionately that Deepavali suited Singapore’s multi-racial fabric better, allowing other races to share in its social joy, whereas Thaipusam remained a strictly intense, specialised Hindu observance.

Noting that Deepavali was a public holiday in India, Pillay insisted the same should apply in the Straits Settlements of Singapore, Penang and Malacca (now Melaka). He added that Indian workers in the PWD and municipal council in Singapore were usually given a holiday on Deepavali day and not Thaipusam day.

The meeting adopted a proposal to send a delegation to convince Governor Young to make Deepavali the public holiday for Hindus in the colony. MV Pillay, who moved the motion, claimed that it was the Chettiar community that was pushing for Thaipusam, and that in doing so it had disregarded the wishes of other communities.

Not everyone agreed with this resolution. Some Singapore Hindus, including those not from the Chettiar community, wrote directly to the governor insisting the original Bill remain unchanged. They claimed that Veerasamy’s group did not speak for everyone and that the government would earn the deep gratitude of the community by following Penang's example.

A fierce but polite battle ensued between supporters of both festivals. Ultimately, the British authorities chose to listen to the Singapore merchant class and the more influential English-speaking elites.
They dropped Thaipusam from the Bill and substituted it with Deepavali, passing the Holidays (Amendment) Ordinance 1914 for the entire colony of Singapore, Penang, and Malacca.

I was unable to find any record that showed strong protests from Penang and Malacca Hindus. I suspect the Chettiars - a small, self-reliant and self-effacing mercantile community that prefers to conduct its business in quiet dignity - decided that Thaipusam would still be observed with due respect even if it was no longer an official holiday.

But the ripple effect soon reached the Federated Malay States (FMS). By April 1915, KT Parmanan Pillay, president of the Sri Mahamariamman Temple on High Street (Jalan Tun HS Lee), wrote to Selangor Resident Edward George Broadrick, telling him that the local Hindu community had passed a resolution asking for both Thaipusam and Deepavali to be declared public holidays.

In Taiping, then the capital of Perak, a public meeting was held in the town hall on Feb 21, 1926 under the chairmanship of H Rethinasamy Pillai, reportedly attended by Indians from several parts of the FMS. The meeting resolved to urge the British authorities to also make Deepavali a public holiday in the FMS, as there was then none for the community.

One of the leaders, V Murugasu Pillai, in a letter to the chief secretary to the FMS government Sir William George Maxwell, noted that Deepavali was already a holiday in the neighbouring Straits Settlements. He claimed that the views of the “Indian and Ceylonese communities” in Selangor, Negri Sembilan and Pahang had also been obtained and that all of them were unanimous in voicing the request for a holiday for Deepavali.

Whether the colonial authorities fully capitulated back then remains slightly murky in the archives, but the framework of history eventually birthed the national holiday we enjoy today under the 1951 Holidays Act.
Today, Deepavali’s lights burn brightly across Malaysia, while in several states, Thaipusam remains a powerful public holiday observed with equal vitality.

Ultimately, the story of Deepavali’s rise is one of quiet endurance rather than conquest. Two great flames once stood at opposite ends of the Hindu night sky—one broad and welcoming, the other focused and sacred. Colonial hands chose one over the other a century ago, but time has proven that neither had to be extinguished.

Today, both Deepavali and Thaipusam light up the Malaysian landscape side by side, proving that traditions fought for with such passion never truly fade. They simply learn to glow together, year after year, across the same land.
Happy Deepavali.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that drew a blank, felt the squeeze, played the queen, and made donkey-bull love.

First, scientists shed new light on how Earth ended up losing more than a billion years of its geological record, a puzzle that has resisted explanation for decades. Then: octopuses in tight spots, a topless spear-brandishing Celt, and a tale of unlikely tail.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
“Blank Space” (Earth’s Version)
Dhungana, Santosh and Flament, Nicolas. “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature.

Earth doesn’t trouble itself too much with keeping intact archives. With its tectonic activity and erosive forces, our planet is constantly wiping out huge chunks of its own memory, creating gaps in the geological record called unconformities.

The Great Unconformity, the largest gap of this kind, reveals that Earth straight-up deleted more than a billion years of strata, for reasons that remain hotly debated and mysterious. Sandstone that dates back to the Cambrian period some 538 million years is often found directly on top of ancient “basement” rocks that date back anywhere from 1.2 billion to 1.8 billion years ago. This missing layer shows up around the world, hinting that it was erased by a global event.
Now, scientists have placed the origins of the Great Unconformity deep inside Earth’s mantle, during the tectonic tumult of supercontinent breakup.

“The cause or causes of the Great Unconformity are unknown,” said authors Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong. “The proposed mechanisms include extensive glacial erosion during Snowball Earth (about 720–635 million years ago), rifting and plume activity, sea-level fall and mantle-driven dynamic topography.”
“These processes have not been dynamically tested, with limited comparison between global models and global datasets to explain the spatial distribution of the Great Unconformity,” the team added.

To fill the knowledge gap about the geological gap, the researchers ran models of the formation and breakup of ancient supercontinents during the eons preceding the Cambrian period, when complex life rapidly proliferated in Earth’s seas. Massive landmasses were pushed upward by motions in Earth’s mantle during this time. Exposed to erosive forces such as weather, glaciers, and eventually oceans, they became sanded down over time, creating the vast void.

“Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes,” the team concluded.

Scientists will no doubt continue to debate the cause of this planet-wide memory lapse, but there is consensus that the same mechanisms also set the stage for the emergence of complex life during the Cambrian. No matter what caused the Great Unconformity, we partly owe our existence to it today.
In other news…
Putting the squeeze on octopuses
Xin, Wenci et al. “Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes.” Journal of Experimental Biology.

We’ll move now from massive gaps in Earth’s memory to tiny gaps that octopuses can somehow squeeze through. These tentacled escape artists can famously maneuver their way through passages that seem impossibly small relative to their bodies, an ability that has spawned a subgenre of viral videos.

Now, scientists have discovered the secrets of “octopus-squeezing behavior” by observing two species—the common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) and the Mayan octopus (Octopus maya)—navigating small holes in laboratory containers.

“Our study demonstrates that octopuses employ two primary strategies, 3-step and 4-step, for squeezing through narrow spaces,” said researchers led by Wenci Xin of the National University of Singapore. “The key distinction between these strategies lies in whether the body is squeezed separately from the arms.”

The first two steps were probing the aperture and then shifting a few arms through it. Navigating the tightest spaces required breaking up the final passage into two parts: Pulling the remaining arms to the other side, and then compressing the mantle behind the head so they could fit through last.
In addition to documenting these amazing feats of flexibility in nature, the study is the perfect excuse to revisit the classic X-Files episode “Squeeze.”
A queen hidden in plain sight?
Russell, Miles. “Verica Rex: Searching for a ‘lost’ queen of the British Iron Age.” Current Archaeology.

When Rome invaded Britain 2,000 years ago, they had the help of an inside man—or was it an inside woman? In a new article, an archaeologist makes the case that the British king Verica, who aided the Roman invasion of their own homeland, was actually a queen that has been misgendered lo these many centuries.

Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues that Verica was a woman based in part on the leader’s Latin name, which ends in the suffix “a” which is common for women, as opposed to names ending in “-us” for men.

Coins also depict Verica using “slender, bare-breasted equestrian figures that appear irrefutably female in contrast to the overtly masculine warriors on the issues of Iron Age rulers like Tasciovanus and Caratacus,” according to Russell.

Many experts are not convinced that the evidence points to a secret ancient queen, and Verica’s gender is likely to inspire much more debate. Wikipedia, our great public arbiter, has not changed Verica’s male pronouns.

Women leaders weren’t unheard of in Celtic Britain, as evidenced by the queens Cartimandua and Boudica, who lived in the same century as Verica. Regardless of whether Verica was among their ranks, this leader was a consequential figure in the Roman takeover of Britain.
Achille and Patroclo: More than friends
Da Cruz, André B et al. “A socio-sexual bond between a bull and a male donkey.” Current Biology.
Scientists who were conducting fieldwork on monkeys in Ethiopia serendipitously stumbled upon a very different discovery—a tender same-sex relationship between a bull and a donkey.

Achille, a bull, and Patroclo, a donkey, belong to different owners, but they graze together by day. Despite the availability of other males and females in their pasture, this pair has developed a strong socio-sexual bond that includes nuzzling, licking, and Achille sexually mounting Patroclo.

“Patroclo frequently presented his hindquarters toward Achille and nipped him,” said researchers led by André Beirão da Cruz of the University of Pisa. “In the only two instances in which Achille approached and mounted another male donkey, this individual showed clear avoidance behaviours and displayed threatening facial expressions (e.g. ear flattening), which were never observed in Patroclo during the 51 mountings (34 with intromission) with Achille.”

Same-sex sexual behavior is extremely common in nature and has a wide variety of possible explanations, including social cohesion, mistaken identity, or lack of access to opposite-sex mates. But what Achille and Patroclo have is special. Despite being different species and having alternate mating options, the pair share a highly selective and reciprocal social and sexual bond.

“Although interpreting this behaviour is challenging, the mounting attempts, taken together with the repeated and mutual affiliative interactions between the two animals, may signal the quality of their relationship” and “the strength of the animals’ social bond,” the team concluded.

In addition to this heartwarming tale, the study goes to show that you never know what you might find when you chase your goals. The researchers were there to watch geladas, but it turned out those primates weren’t the only animals monkeying around.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.

ca8187dc18d8d6b4: From P Kamalanathan

Deepavali is here again. In every Hindu home, the oil lamps are lit, the kolam is drawn, the house is filled with the smell of murukku, nei urundai and payasam, and children run around in new clothes, waiting for the first burst of fireworks.
But beyond the celebration, Deepavali carries a timeless message that we must never forget: Light must triumph over darkness.
Thiruvalluvar said it beautifully more than 2,000 years ago:
Those who seek the Divine will be freed from the darkness of life.
That darkness is not just outside us. It is also within us; anger, jealousy, hatred, selfishness, and division.
Deepavali reminds us to light a lamp inside ourselves first.
Deepavali is also a celebration of our identity

For Malaysians of Indian origin, Deepavali is not just a festival. It is a reminder of who we are, where we come from, and what we carry forward for our children. Our language, our culture, our values, our faith, these are the lamps we must keep burning.

Just this week, we saw how important it is to protect that light. When there was a proposal to reduce Tamil language hours in our Tamil schools from 12 to 10 periods, our community spoke up together; teachers, parents, PTAs, leaders, and ordinary families. And I am grateful that the education ministry listened and decided not to pursue it.
That is the spirit of Deepavali. When we stand together in light, darkness cannot win.
Deepavali is a Malaysian celebration

In Malaysia, Deepavali is not celebrated only by Indians. Our Malay, Chinese, Kadazan, Iban and Orang Asli friends join us at our open houses, taste our food, wear Indian clothes, and share our joy. That is the true beauty of Malaysia, unity in diversity, not just in words, but in our homes.

As a former deputy education minister, I have always believed that our greatest strength is our children. If we teach them to respect all races and religions, to love their own mother tongue while embracing Bahasa Malaysia and English, to be kind and to be disciplined; then Malaysia’s future will be bright.
This Deepavali, let us make three promises:
1. Light a lamp for unity Let us reject hatred and division, and choose understanding.
2. Light a lamp for education Let us encourage our children to study hard, to read our mother tongue language, to master knowledge, and to be proud of their heritage.
3. Light a lamp for kindness Let us remember the poor, the lonely, and those who are struggling. Share a meal. Visit an old folks’ home. Help a neighbour. That is the true Deepavali.
To all Malaysians, I wish you a Happy Deepavali.
May your home be filled with light, your family with love, and your life with health and prosperity.
P Kamalanathan is a former deputy education minister and an FMT reader.

2172131c972baeee: Saya angkat songkok kepada Umno sambil ucap tahniah dan syabas kerana berjaya kutip RM50 juta dengan cepat dan pantas bagi membolehkan bekas presiden Najib Razak menjalani baki hukuman penjara di rumah.
Kita tentu masih ingat Umno mula pungut wang September lalu. Semalam RM50 juta sudah dapat dikumpulkan. Kurang tiga bulan. Satu pencapaian menakjubkan.

Itu sebab saya kata Umno 'terer'. Power. Orang lain terkial-kial cari dana untuk capai sasaran jauh yang lebih kurang daripada jumlah yang Umno kumpulkan dengan mudah. Misalnya, ada banyak NGO bertungkus-lumus cari sumbangan orang ramai dan syarikat untuk umpamanya membiayai pembedahan jantung kanak-kanak. Media juga diminta membantu untuk menghebahkan usaha mereka supaya matlamat tercapai. Usaha itu mungkin membuahkan hasil tetapi ada kala mengambil masa berbulan-bulan atau lebih lama.

Tetapi Umno dapat pungut RM50 juta bagai sekelip mata, menyebabkan saya angkat songkok dengan penuh rasa kagum. Saya cadang NGO minta pertolongan Umno lain kali mahu cari dana untuk biaya rawatan pesakit yang tidak berkemampuan, atau belajar daripada Umno rahsia memungut wang dengan pantas.

To put things in context, kita imbau kembali. Najib dipenjarakan pada Ogos 2022 selepas Mahkamah Persekutuan mengekalkan sabitan atas kesalahan menyalahguna kuasa, pecah amanah dan pengubahan wang haram membabitkan dana RM42 juta milik SRC International. Beliau dihukum penjara 12 tahun dan denda RM210 juta.

Pun begitu pada Januari 2024, Yang di-Pertuan Agong ketika itu Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah mengurangkan separuh hukuman itu dan menurunkan jumlah denda kepada RM50 juta menerusi pengampunan diraja. Pada September lalu, Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim memberikan Najib pengampunan bersyarat yang membolehkan dia menjalani baki hukuman di bawah tahanan rumah sehingga 23 Ogos 2028.

Tetapi tahanan di rumah hanya boleh dilaksanakan jika Najib bayar denda RM50 juta serta pematuhan syarat-syarat lain yang ditetapkan. Syarat-syarat itu membabitkan urusan pemenjaraan. Yang paling utama ialah Najib mesti bayar RM50 juta, barulah boleh nikmati tahanan di rumah, di kediaman yang terletak di kawasan elit di ibu negara.

Berikutan itu, Umno lancar Tabung Solidariti Najib Razak pada 18 Sept lalu, tujuannya untuk kumpul RM50 juta. Menurut Setiausaha Agung Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki, setakat Ogos lalu, Wanita Umno ada 1,412,052 ahli. Pemuda Umno ada 418,062 ahli. Puteri Umno pula 226,076 ahli. Jadi jumlah keseluruhan ahli Umno ialah 3,251,456 orang.

Saya tidak tahu sama ada si setiausaha agung Umno ada ambil kira jumlah ahli yang tinggalkan parti. Lazimnya orang yang keluar parti akan angkat kaki begitu sahaja. Mereka tidak akan maklumkan kepada ibu pejabat Umno. Saya merujuk kepada ahli biasa yang tak terkenal.

Tidak usah pertikai jumlah ahli Umno yang diumumkan si setiausaha agung parti. Take it as it is, ertinya ada tiga juta lebih ahli. Senang cerita genapkan kepada empat juta ahli Umno maka jika setiap ahli sumbang RM1 untuk tabung Najib, dapat kumpul RM4 juta sahaja. Bagaimanapun takkanlah mereka sumbang RM1 sahaja -- mungkin ada yang sumbang RM50, RM100 atau RM1,000. Tentu ada yang beri lebih daripada itu.

Teringat saya laporan media 21 Sept lalu yang memetik isteri Najib, Rosmah Mansor, menzahirkan rasa terharu kerana rakan-rakan dari Singapura, Brunei, Itali dan Kanada menghulur sumbangan untuk bantu Najib. Mungkin jumlah yang dinyatakan Rosmah itu disalurkan kepada tabung anjuran Umno.

Sememangnya RM50 juta itu satu jumlah besar. Semalam Asyraf dengan bangga dan gembira mengumumkan partinya sudah berjaya kumpul dana mencukupi menerusi kempen sumbangan untuk Najib, dan Umno sudah menjelaskan denda RM50 juta untuk Najib.
"Kami ingin mengucapkan terima kasih kepada ahli-ahli dan orang ramai atas sumbangan mereka," kata Asyraf menerusi kenyataan.

Muncul bekas Ahli Parlimen Damansara Tony Pua menggesa pihak berkuasa mengaudit sumbangan yang dikutip. Kata beliau, audit oleh Bank Negara dan Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia penting bagi memastikan dana yang dikumpulkan diperoleh secara sah dan bukan hasil pengubahan wang haram. Saya setuju.
Dalam pada itu, Pua berpendapat adalah lebih elok jika wang yang Umno kumpul digunakan untuk bantu rakyat biasa. Memang betul tetapi jelas Umno has its own priorities.

f4409c2630f1bd35: From Moaz Nair

We must all extend our heartfelt gratitude to PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang. For decades, ordinary Malaysians have blundered through political disagreements using tedious, secular terms like "policy differences", "economic discrepancies" or "constitutional debates". How utterly pedestrian.

As a vanguard of religious leadership, the PAS supremo has single-handedly elevated local political discourse into an apocalyptic battleground. While political analysts and opposition figures may fret over his "highly polarising language", they simply lack the vision to appreciate the sheer artistry of his negative vocabulary. For those trying to understand how a man so deeply versed in Islam chooses to navigate the political arena, here is a handy guide to his masterclass in decorum.
'Dajjal' doctrine

Why debate the terms of a standard legislative agreement when you can invoke the literal embodiment of evil? In November, when the government and opposition floated a routine confidence and supply agreement, ordinary leaders might have debated fiscal allocations. Not the maestro. Hadi swiftly diagnosed the cross-party truce as a "Dajjal approach at the end of times". By equating a political compromise to the false Messiah, he reminded us all that bipartisanship isn't just bad governance – it is practically the precursor to Armageddon.
Advanced sociology

In 2022, Hadi gracefully simplified the complex, systemic issue of financial crime. While anti-corruption agencies waste millions studying institutional loopholes, Hadi cracked the code by declaring non-Muslims and non-Bumiputeras the "roots of corruption" in Malaysia. When civil society groups like Transparency International Malaysia cried foul over xenophobia, they clearly missed the theological nuance: why fix a broken system when you can just blame a demographic?
Grammar lessons

Parliamentary decorum is so last century. In 2025, during a serious parliamentary debate, Hadi decided to give the Dewan Rakyat a live lesson in the finer points of the national language. When referring to a small group of white Westerners, he bypassed standard human pronouns entirely and opted for the animal classifier "ekor" (tails). While lawmakers questioned his basic courtesy, language purists had to admire his commitment to treating geopolitical adversaries like stray livestock.
Intellectual plebeians

Consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds. When four Malay DAP leaders had the audacity to question Hadi's shifting ideological stances over the years, he didn’t bother wasting precious scripture on them. Instead, he publicly dismissed them as "kurang berpendidikan" (uneducated). It is a flawless debate tactic: if someone points out an inconsistency, simply remind them they lack the spiritual PhD required to comprehend it.
Friendship flexibility

Over the decades, the PAS supremo has treated political alliances like fashion seasons – highly disposable and entirely dependent on the weather. Consider his decades-long dance with DAP. During the golden years of the Barisan Alternatif and Pakatan Rakyat coalitions (1999–2013), Hadi shared the stage with the very same DAP leaders he now rebukes. Back then, political cooperation (tahaluf siyasi) was championed as a noble, strategic pursuit.

Fast forward to the 2015 PAS muktamar, where the party abruptly severed ties with DAP without debate. Overnight, the former allies were retroactively transformed into the ultimate ideological adversaries. Progressive PAS members who dared to question this sudden U-turn were thoroughly purged, eventually leaving to form the splinter party Amanah.

The flexibility didn't stop there. By 2019, Hadi had signed the Muafakat Nasional pact with Umno – the absolute arch-nemesis his infamous 1981 "Amanat Hadi" had once forcefully condemned. By 2020, he pivoted again to anchor Perikatan Nasional. It is a masterclass in situational theology: an alliance is perfectly holy right up until the exact moment it becomes politically inconvenient, at which point it is scrubbed from historical memory.
Political safari

When he is not channelling the end-times, our grand maestro moonlights as a visionary political safari guide, earning the fond moniker of an "amateur zoologist". Under his taxonomic eye, a battered Umno was famously diagnosed as a hobbled "itik patah kaki" (lame duck) to justify PAS seizing the steering wheel.

Meanwhile, secular opportunists and those demanding Western-style updates are swiftly demoted to "binatang yang tidak berakal" (senseless animals). Should you dare criticise his shifting paradigms, you are seamlessly categorised into his menagerie as either a hyperactive "kera" (monkey), a relentlessly barking "anjing" (dog) or a "babi" (pig). Naturally, this rich pedagogical blueprint has inspired his disciples – PAS lawmakers recently took flight into the aviary, branding Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim a "burung tiong" (myna bird) to mock him as a mindless echo chamber for external policies.
Linguistic irony

This leads us to the ultimate comedic paradox of modern Malaysian politics: the profound irony of utilising the sacred vocabulary of the heavens to conduct everyday, transactional mud-slinging. Islam possesses a rich linguistic tradition designed to inspire spiritual contemplation and universal grace. Yet, in the hands of the PAS leadership, this vocabulary is weaponised as a highly specialised political toolkit.

When routine legislative agreements are framed through the lens of Islamic eschatology, a standard, secular agreement is artificially inflated into a cosmic battle between divine light and ultimate darkness. By deploying heavy theological concepts to score cheap points in the daily 24-hour news cycle, the sacred is systematically cheapened.

The greatest irony lies in the moral inversion it creates. While the faith heavily emphasises humility, restraint and the avoidance of slander, this brand of political rhetoric uses the language of the faith to justify the exact opposite: alienating minor demographics, dismissing critics as intellectually inferior and reducing foreign visitors to animal classifiers.
Entertaining spectacle

While monitoring bodies like the Centre for Independent Journalism track his vocabulary as a major driver of identity-based division, defenders stand firm, arguing this uncompromising tone is a steadfast defence of faith.

And who can blame them? Nothing screams "peaceful, universal faith" quite like reducing your neighbours to corrupt roots, your parliamentary colleagues to animals and basic governance to the work of the false Messiah.

Ultimately, this strategy yields a highly entertaining spectacle. By insisting that every standard political manoeuvre is either an act of divine necessity or a plot by the Dajjal, the political arena becomes an absurdist theatre – proving that nothing elevates a secular turf war quite like a heavy dusting of fire and brimstone.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

6759006f0ed19363: Right now, Leonard Cohen is on many of his fans’ minds. The Canadian poet, novelist and singer-songwriter died Nov. 7, 2016, just one day before United States President Donald Trump was first elected. Ten years later, as the Democrat “blue wave” hopes to close the bracket on a president who once memed himself as Jesus personified, Cohen’s legacy has become effortlessly epic — even biblical — in quite a different way. Tribute gatherings Tribute gatherings for the singer abound. Cohen was the subject of a sold-out event at the Toronto International Festival of Authors at the end of October. Adam Cohen’s family tour, which began in Canada this month and reaches Europe in winter 2027, pairs his father’s music with archival photos and film. Ottawa’s Gladstone Theatre advertised their “Ten Years Gone” commemoration with a question quite suggestive to people like me who study the evolution of sacred texts: “What would Cohen say today?” Cohen’s ‘contemporary psalms’ As an answer, I highlight an under-celebrated part of Cohen’s poetry and song. As I detail in my 2023 book Prophets of Love: The Unlikely Kinship of Leonard Cohen and the Apostle Paul, all of Cohen’s work is infused with biblical allusions. But some of Cohen’s work does more than echo biblical themes. It takes on biblical format, in the tradition of poetic prayer known in Hebrew as tehillim. Tehillim, or Psalms, inform the Jewish liturgical tradition of addressing God directly, not only in praise, but also in lament, desperation and challenge. This is most explicit in what publisher McClelland and Stewart called Cohen’s “contemporary psalms” in his Book of Mercy. In 1984, as Cohen turned 50, his life provided the material for the 50 psalms of lament, complaint, joy, doubt, adoration and desperation that made up this poetry collection. Like the biblical Psalms, these short poems are numbered rather than titled. Cohen described the collection as “meant for people like myself who could use it, at a particular time,” as “a book of prayer.” Many interpreters continue to analyze this collection as Tehillim. Writing liturgy Although modest about himself in public, Cohen never lacked ambition for his poetry. Rabbi Mordecai Finley, who has read Cohen’s poems aloud for High Holy Days, recalls Cohen confiding that he felt he was always writing not just poetry, but liturgy. Ben Sales points out that Cohen’s song “If It Be Your Will” echoes the Friday evening prayer service welcoming Shabbat, and “Who By Fire” is a nearly word-for-word arrangement of the High Holiday prayer, the “Unetaneh Tokef.” Cohen’s “Anthem,” with its famous line “that’s how the light gets in,” inspires ponderings from both Christians and Jews. And “Hallelujah,” — a biblical term heard in church services — is a star example of a Cohen song as religious anthem, despite its references to surprisingly carnal biblical texts. I believe Cohen’s grappling with the divine, whether overt, or nestled within his sensual poetry, might prove to be his most enduring memorial. Multiple traditions and levels Cohen biographer and author Harry Freedman reports that Cohen studied in India, referenced the Kabbalah frequently and knew the lore of the Christian Desert Mothers and Fathers. Both Kabbalah and early Christian ascetics blur the boundaries between the erotic and the divine. Cohen’s way of addressing the sensual and the spiritual simultaneously allows the same song to reach different people — or reach the same person at different times. He could also speak from multiple traditions. Cohen was an ordained Rinzai Zen monk, the grandson of a famous rabbi and Talmud scholar. As an impressionable child he went to mass with his Irish nanny in Montréal, a city of churches. In I’m Your Man, music journalist Sylvie Simmons chronicles how Cohen was a deeply knowledgeable Jew who moved comfortably between the Torah, Talmud, Tao Te Ching, Sufi mysticism and the New Testament. No religious tourist Fewer Canadians remember the literary critic Northrop Frye than know Cohen. But the poet turned out to be the perfect example of the professor’s point: the educated imagination lives and breathes the vocabulary of the sacred. Cohen was no religious tourist. Rather, the singer “spoke multiple religions” fluently, always from his Jewish roots. At this 10th yahrzeit of his passing, it’s worth considering to whom (besides his audiences) he addressed his final performances. In “Traveling Light,” from You Want it Darker, he sang: “But if the road leads back to you, Must I forget the things I knew …Traveling light, like we used to do.” Grappling with God Like the ultimate Psalmist, King David, dethroned and on the run, Cohen was at a low point in his career when he wrote Book of Mercy. In those dark days of seeming failure, before Jennifer Warnes’s Famous Blue Raincoat revived his career, Book of Mercy was the middle-aged Jewish poet’s attempt to leave at least something of permanence: “We talk in this manner, we sing the time-honoured songs, and we compose new ones, as we were commanded,” he wrote in “25.” Yet, for me, it is Cohen’s final albums 20 and 30 years later, as his life neared its end, that most resemble the Psalms in how they grapple with God. Psalms for every human experience Through the years, Cohen addressed God right before our eyes in the person of a lover. At the end of his life, he boldly exposed the relationship that had been there all along — perhaps most notably in the song “You Want it Darker.” Here, he addressed God as “My lord,” incorporated elements of the Jewish mourners’ prayer and adapted Rosh Hashanah liturgy. Was Cohen writing and adapting Kaddish for his own impending death? I believe so, although in true Cohen fashion his words also mourn humanity overall, and challenge the divine. Leonard Cohen’s ‘You Want it Darker.’ As I wrote in Prophets of Love, for Leonard as “Cohen” (Hebrew for priest), existential longing and divine connection are inseparably linked at the base of the human condition. So, 10 years later, even if you are already a devotee, have a listen again. Pay special attention to how Cohen challenges, pleads with, chastises and even woos the divine. If you are not yet a fan, buy one of the iconic Canadian’s final albums, when he could feel death waiting at the door. You may find that, just as for many faithful opening the ancient psalms, there’s material in Cohen’s contemporary psalms for every human experience, including yours. ba5f1cdb14f57903: Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it’s pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs, or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it’s also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave in terms of the myriad different properties and responses materials can exhibit. Recent progress has been made on using artificial intelligence and machine learning to supplement or speed up laborious calculations based on physical principles that can at least provide some initial guidance on which compounds might be worth synthesizing and testing. Now, a new method developed at MIT shows that when there are few data on some technologically relevant property, such as ligand affinities for a recently discovered cellular target for a potential drug, this approach can outperform other existing methods for winnowing down the field of possible molecules that might be worth looking at. The findings were reported in the Sept. 14 issue of the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling, in a paper by MIT graduate student Akshat Shirish Zalte and recent graduate Jackson Burns PhD ’26, Research Scientist Charlles Abreu, Professor William Green, and three researchers from the chemical company BASF.  An earlier version of the paper has been online since last year, and the open-source model the team developed, called CheMeleon, has already found regular use by several pharmaceutical companies. CheMeleon was built using ChemProp, an open-source machine-learning package also developed and maintained by the Green group at MIT, and anyone can download CheMeleon through ChemProp and fine-tune it for their own purposes. Earlier this year, there was a contest organized by OpenADMET for trying to predict the properties of a variety of new molecules that had not previously been synthesized, says Green, who is the Hoyt Hottel Professor of Chemical Engineering. “It was a big contest, a lot of people participated,” he says. When the winners were announced, it turned out that nine of the top 20 entries had used CheMeleon in their process. “So then we started getting all kinds of inquiries from the pharma companies about this, but our paper had just been submitted; it wasn’t even peer-reviewed or anything yet.” While the paper went through that review process, its influence was already spreading. At least one pharma company, Green says, “sent a message to all their people, and said ‘Anytime you’re modeling a property, start with CheMeleon, that’s our new company policy’” when making initial decisions about which molecules to pursue. The key to CheMeleon was pre-training a machine-learning model with detailed data about a million different molecules, so that it gets to learn correlations between the structure of a given molecule and how it behaves with respect to a catalog of about 1,600 descriptors that have been developed by chemists over decades. CheMeleon can then be fine-tuned to predict well-known properties like solubility and viscosity, to more esoteric properties such as bioactivity or reactivity, with a certain protein or enzyme. Those million molecules are a minuscule fraction of the innumerable ways that atoms can bond together, but they provide enough examples so that once the AI system has been trained on them, it can work out on its own many underlying patterns and relationships, and then apply those to a new, unknown molecule that’s presented to it. “Most of today’s deep-learning models require more data than traditional methods,” says Zalte. Some successful models use extensive data from the published literature in chemical journals, he says. “We don’t look at the literature at all. We just calculate a bunch of molecular descriptors like molecular weight or number of oxygens, among others.” Then predicting those descriptors forms the basis for their pre-training task. CheMeleon is a pre-trained foundation model. Inspired by the well-known foundation models in language such as ChatGPT and Claide, which essentially are developed by feeding them massive amounts of information from the internet, CheMeleon uses molecular descriptors of a million molecules from PubChem, a large, freely available database of chemical information maintained by the U.S. National Institutes of Health.  With classical expert-driven models, on the other hand, specialists in a field manually input detailed knowledge about their subject. In developing these classical models, he says, for example, people know from experiments that a certain property of interest, say solubility, may relate to particular descriptors of the same molecules, “like molecular weight, or the number of oxygens that are present, or how branchy or bulky the molecule is.”  With this team’s approach, they can start with an existing neural network architecture and train it to learn underlying principles. “We’re not training it for a specific property, but as a general model that understands some level of chemistry, so that even if you fine-tune it with just a few data points for the task you care about, you can still get some good performance,” he says. That’s thanks to the fact that the model is “not having to learn everything from scratch.” To verify its usefulness, “We compared our model not only against other foundation models that are out there, but also with classical models leveraging expert-designed principles,” Zalte says. Comparing its performance across 58 test cases, “we see that our model comes out on top.” Green adds, “The CheMeleon foundation model drastically reduces the number of molecules that need to be tested experimentally to accurately predict the properties of new molecules. This is a huge advantage, since synthesizing and testing a large number of molecules is slow and expensive." Besides the MIT members, the team also included Jochen Sieg, Christian Feldmann, and Miriam Mathea, researchers at BASF SE in Germany. The work was supported by the Machine Learning for Pharmaceutical Discovery and Synthesis consortium, along with fellowship support from U.S. Department of Energy and MathWorks.
3e5ae70a61891983: On the eve of Donald Trump’s return to the presidency of the United States, in January 2025, Meta’s founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that changes would be made to his company’s moderation policies in the name of “freedom of expression”, which, he said, was under threat by global pressures for what he saw as censorship. The announcement signaled a rapprochement between Meta and the far right around a common goal: the deregulation of Big Tech. Since then, growing entanglement between major technology companies and the U.S. President Donald Trump administration has shown how the private interests of a small group can override the public interest. In recent months, allegations have been mounting that Big Tech companies, especially Meta, have been interfering in the Brazilian electoral process this year, aiming to undermine the reelection of President Lula (PT). This kind of accusation is not new. Over the past decade, a vast body of literature has exposed the mediating role played by digital platforms in foreign interference in elections around the world. These reports have also highlight the challenges of holding companies accountable for allowing these interference campaigns to be amplified. At our research group, NetLab UFRJ, we have spent years investigating how major digital platforms shape public debate and influence people’s perceptions of reality, often outside the regulatory and normative frameworks in force in Brazil. Meta in particular has become fertile ground for disinformation and boosting fraudulent ads, which already account for 10% of its annual revenue. Despite lawsuits and administrative actions brought by Brazilian authorities against Meta, complaints and requests from civil society for investigations, as well as reports published by the press, the company has shown neither the willingness nor the diligence needed to effectively fight this kind of content. Given this troubling track record, NetLab UFRJ created the “Big Tech Observatory” during the 2026 election campaign period in order to monitor how Meta and other digital platforms performed in two key areas: algorithmic recommendation and political advertising. The initiative set out to examine whether these companies would comply with the current Brazilian legislation established by the Electoral Supreme Court (TSE). The results of the analyses, however, told a predictable story. We found that, between July and September, Meta received approximately R$ 2 million (US$ 400,000) for running 1,613 ads placed from outside Brazil that aimed to either favor or harm candidates. All were paid for in foreign currencies and boosted by pages with declared locations in other countries. The amount invested in this advertising is equivalent to that spent on prominent campaigns, including the race for Presidency and other executive offices. Brazilian electoral law expressly prohibits candidates from receiving cash or donations in-kind from abroad. This ban, however, did not prevent the ads from being displayed to Brazilian users of Meta’s platforms. According to the available information, not only the ads were allowed to circulate but they may have reached up to 171 million views in the country. But the irregularities in advertising do not stop there. Brazilian electoral rules prohibit electoral advertising from 48 hours before the polls to 24 hours afterwards. However, our analyses of both rounds of the 2026 election identified hundreds of ads in favor or against specific candidates that circulated on Meta’s platforms with no apparent restrictions. The company even allowed fake profiles posing as official channels of the Electoral Supreme Court to boost disinformation about a supposed “digital vote” which stated that people would be allowed to cast their vote from home on the day of the first round — something which does not exist in the Brazilian electoral system. In addition to these irregularities, Lula’s political campaign page was temporarily disabled by Meta without explanation, preventing it from running electoral ads. On September 23, his Worker´s Party (PT) reported they had been blocked from advertising on Meta’s platforms. In a statement released on October 16, the company rejected the accusations of election interference and attributed the temporary deactivation to an “incorrect anti-fraud review” carried out under an agreement with the federal government to fight fraud involving public programs. The effectiveness of the company’s anti-fraud measures, however, is questionable: an analysis carried out by NetLab UFRJ identified hundreds of fraudulent ads involving federal public policies circulating before and after September 23, indicating that those same measures were not able to stop this kind of content from running during the same period. Finally, we found signs of discriminatory practices in ad pricing. Based on data released by Meta, we estimate that for the first round Lula’s campaign may have paid between 33% and 43% more than his far right adversary Flávio Bolsonaro campaign to reach the same number of users on Meta’s platforms. Despite this substantial difference, limitations in the company’s transparency policies make it impossible to identify precisely which parameters and criteria are used to price ads and, consequently, to draw definitive conclusions about the mechanisms behind this disparity. Even so, studies conducted in other contexts, such as the United States, India and the Netherlands, also point to evidence of discriminatory pricing practices in the platform’s advertising. Other complaints made during the elections add to this overall scenario of negligence and show that, despite being worth billions and their strategic position at the forefront of technological innovation, major digital platforms invest little in protecting their users. For example, this 2026 election in Brazil saw several controversies involving WhatsApp’s image generation service, powered by the Meta AI artificial intelligence. Users reported being able to generate content favorable to Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign without difficulty, whereas they were not getting the same results for Lula. Meanwhile, the documentary channel Revelando had videos criticizing Flávio Bolsonaro removed from its Instagram profiles shortly after they were posted, without clear justification from the company. These episodes cast doubt on the consistency of Meta’s moderation and content control systems, exposing failures that call for greater investment and improvement. The situation is made worse by the absence of transparent criteria or guarantees of equal treatment in how ads are handled, how content is recommended, how advertising is priced, and how profiles and posts are moderated. Big Tech companies have developed predatory business models, and they are currently joining forces with political forces committed to deregulation in Brazil. This is part of a strategy to protect their businesses and expand their room for maneuver. Whether or not one side of the electoral race is being deliberately favored, it is indisputable that the major digital platforms continuously exercise the power to determine what gains visibility and what remains on the margins, with no transparency over their criteria and no mechanism for accountability. What is clear is that, for these platforms, defending their economic interests and maximizing their profits prevails above user rights, public interest, and democracy itself. 55f50804082a4644: <!--kg-card-end: html--> This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss election outcomes and code as a human endeavor.

JOSEPH: This week I got a real wave of ‘oh man this fucking sucks’ regarding AI. I won’t link to it because it’s just a rando person, but scrolling Reddit I saw someone who said they used Claude to build stuff with Max. Max, or Max/MSP, is a visual programming language that is heavily used in the world of music and visual art. It is the foundation of a lot of electronic music. You can build essentially anything in it, if you put in the work to understand how to put it together. And that can be a lot of work.

I’ve built various little things in Max. I made a tool that takes a drum break and generates new, random drum and bass style breaks from it. I am a big, big fan of generative music (both listening and making) where you create rules and parameters, press play, and let the rules decide what comes out. I made another that has various synthesizers, and from scratch manipulates the audio so they sound like Tibetan singing bowls, with their harmonies and individual melodies morphing over time. I also started working on the visual part of Max, called Jitter, to take audio output from Max and generate visuals.
1bd5c4dc6b5408a4: The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, will get underway in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9. One of its key objectives is to boost electrification across the global economy – replacing petrol and diesel vehicles, gas boilers and some industrial processes that burn fossil fuels with electric alternatives. The summit’s host, Turkey, has set a target of 35% of energy demand being met by electricity by 2035, up from around 20% today. Announcing the “35-by-35” pledge, Cop31 president Murat Kurum described it as “one of the defining features” of Turkey’s presidency, highlighting the risks of continued dependence on imported fossil fuels. Without doubt, electrification is essential to curtailing greenhouse gas emissions, and is already gathering pace. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has declared we are living in the “age of electricity”, and if stated policy pledges hold, global electrification rates will hit 31% by 2050. The Cop31’s focus on electrification hopes to build upon and accelerate this existing trend. But electrification alone won’t deliver a clean energy transition. Two major challenges remain: the continued expansion of fossil fuel production, and growing geopolitical competition over clean technologies where the latter is increasingly shaping governments’ climate and energy policies, as they struggle to compete with dominant “electrostates” such as China. Silence on supply The Australian climate minister and Cop31’s president of negotiations has described electrification and fossil fuel reduction as “different sides of the same coin”. But they are not interchangeable. Electrification can reduce some demand for fossil fuels, but it won’t stop governments approving new projects and expanding supply. By 2030, governments are planning to produce more than double the amount of fossil fuels than would be consistent with limiting warning to 1.5°C. More concerning is that this assessment was made before the conflict and disruption in the Middle East, which has caused the US, Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada and other fossil fuel producers to increase output in the name of energy security. The UK, meanwhile, has approved the Jackdaw gasfield in a purported bid to protect jobs and keep homes warm. The 35-by-35 target is also silent on where that additional electricity will come from. After all, a country could in theory increase its rate of electrification by burning more fossil fuels (imagine a country where every car was electric, but all that electricity came from coal). A genuine energy transition What’s needed is the two-pronged approach of electrifying economies while simultaneously phasing out fossil fuels and reducing their supply. This will ensure capital is reallocated to renewable energy for electrification. Governments can do this nationally or through international initiatives such as the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance, the Clean Energy Transition Partnership and the Cop-adjacent conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels. Skirting the fossil fuel issue is nothing new at these summits. It took 26 years for a formal resolution or agreement to explicitly name fossil fuels, in Glasgow in 2021. And even then it only passed with calls to “phasedown” unabated coal power and phase-out “inefficient” fossil fuel subsidies. At Cop31, fossil fuels are entirely absent from the formal agenda. Brazil has published an extensive voluntary “roadmap” to guide governments’ phase-out efforts, but this sits outside the formal negotiations and lacks timelines. This begs the question: is a focus on electrification a way to avoid the perennially thorny issue of fossil fuels? Just electrify everything Even growing demand for electricity does not guarantee a clean energy transition. The data centre boom in the US and beyond, for instance, is driving the use of gas and coal to generate electricity. The International Gas Union, a lobby group for natural gas producers, is explicitly positioning gas as a way to meet growing demand from data centres and AI. Increasing electrification looks relatively straightforward: just encourage more renewable energy production and electric vehicles. Yet, for most of the world, this would mean overcoming security and trade tensions with China, whose dominance in clean technologies, manufacturing and rare earth processing makes it a lynchpin electrostate in a world hoping to electrify everything. China’s dominance is near total. For the component materials of solar panels, in 2024 China controlled 93% of global polysilicon processing, 97% of wafer manufacturing – making the thin slices of silicon that form the basis of solar panels – 92% of solar cell manufacturing and 86% of solar module production. It also produced more than 80% of electric vehicle batteries in 2025. According to the IEA, China is dominant across 19 of 20 energy-related strategic minerals, averaging over 70% of processing control. Achieving global electrification targets will therefore require continued access to Chinese technologies, products and raw materials. This runs counter to almost two decades of western policy aimed at protecting domestic industries from Chinese competition and restricting China’s technological development, most notably with semi-conductors. While these efforts have largely failed to contain Chinese innovation, an overreliance on Chinese clean technologies is increasingly seen as a “serious risk” to Europe’s economic and national security. European governments have responded with tariffs and restrictions on Chinese imports and investments, while seeking to build up their own manufacturing capacity. Governments face a difficult dilemma. Opening their economies further to Chinese technologies could mean unpicking trade protections developed over years and create new dependencies, while refusing to cooperate with China risks slowing electrification and may even drive some governments to abandon climate and energy policies altogether because they cannot compete. While the drive towards electrification at Cop31 is to be welcomed, it cannot be a substitute for the harder political task of securing binding commitments to phase out fossil fuels, fast and fairly.
